blocks.text: 10.4.4. Annotation Processing and Code Generation

The order service finds its commands at startup: it scans the class path for classes marked `@Command("refund")`, `@Command("audit")` and so on, and creates each one through its no-arg constructor. A refactoring made `Audit`'s constructor private. The build passed, every test that didn't create an `Audit` passed, and the service failed in production on the first `audit` request.

An annotation processor moves that work into the compile. javac runs it; it writes the registry as Java source and can refuse the bad class before anything ships. Declaring annotations is unit 10.4.2 and retention is unit 10.4.3: a processor reads source, so `RetentionPolicy.SOURCE` is enough for `@Command`. Reading annotations at run time through reflection is units 10.3.1 to 10.3.4.
A Processor Is Code javac Runs During the Compile, and What It Adds Is New Source Files
The annotation, and a processor that writes the registry, `app.CommandIndex`, as a `switch` over the command names:

The application has `Refund`, marked `@Command("refund")`, and a `Main` that calls `CommandIndex.create(args[0]).run()`. No file in the application declares `CommandIndex`. The processor is compiled first, on its own, and named when the application is compiled (`out/proc` is on `-cp` too, because the sources import `proc.Command`):

`getElementsAnnotatedWith` returns `Element`s from `javax.lang.model`, the compiler's view of the declarations. The application's classes aren't compiled yet, so there are no `Class` objects. The file the `Filer` creates is compiled along with the sources, which is why `Main` compiled. With `-proc:none` the same compile fails:

app/src/app/Main.java:5: error: cannot find symbol
        CommandIndex.create(args[0]).run();
        ^
  symbol:   variable CommandIndex
  location: class Main
1 error
A processor can also be found without `-processor`, through a file `META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor` in its jar that names the class: the `ServiceLoader` file of unit 8.1.5.

**Discovery changed after Java 21.** With that jar only on `-cp`, javac 21 ran the processor and printed a note that "a future release of javac may disable annotation processing unless at least one processor is specified by name (-processor), or a search path is specified (--processor-path, --processor-module-path), or annotation processing is enabled explicitly (-proc:only, -proc:full)". javac 25, given the same command, ran no processor and failed with the `cannot find symbol` above. Name the processor or the processor path in the build, or pass `-proc:full`.
An Error Reported at the Element Makes javac Point at the User's Line
Now `Audit` from the opening is in the sources, with its private constructor. Before reading on: where does the compile fail, and which file does the error name?

out/gen/app/CommandIndex.java:6: error: Audit() has private access in Audit
            case "audit" -> new app.Audit();
                            ^
1 error

The build fails, but the error is in a file the developer never wrote and may not know exists. The processor should check what the generated code needs, and report a problem through the `Messager`, passing the element that has it:

Here `type` is the `TypeElement`, and `hasPublicNoArgConstructor` looks through `ElementFilter.constructorsIn(type.getEnclosedElements())` for one with no parameters and the `public` modifier. The same compile:

app/src/app/Audit.java:6: error: @Command class needs a public no-arg constructor
public class Audit implements Runnable {
       ^
1 error
A message of kind `ERROR` fails the compile: javac exited with 1 and wrote no class files. A `WARNING` or a `NOTE` leaves the build passing, unless it runs with `-Werror`.

Without the element argument the location is lost: javac printed `error: @Command class needs a public no-arg constructor` with no file and no line, and in a large build you can't tell which class. Throwing from `process` stops javac with `An annotation processor threw an uncaught exception.` and a stack trace through `com.sun.tools.javac`, and exit code 3 instead of 1.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Processing Runs in Rounds, and a Generated File Is Processed in the Next One
A second processor in the build, `CrudProcessor`, generates a delete command for every entity marked `@Crud`. For `Customer` it writes:

That class carries `@Command`, but it doesn't exist when `IndexProcessor` reads the sources. Here the index processor keeps every `@Command` it sees in a field, `found`, and logs each call with a call counter and the simple names of the round's root elements and `@Command` classes:

Note: round 1: roots [Customer, Main, Refund], @Command [Refund], over=false
Note: round 2: roots [DeleteCustomer], @Command [DeleteCustomer], over=false
Note: round 3: roots [], @Command [], over=true

Round 1 hands the processors the sources. Every file created in a round is an input of the next round, so `DeleteCustomer` arrives in round 2, where its `@Command` is seen. Rounds go on until one creates nothing, and then a last round runs with no inputs and `processingOver()` true.

The `Processor` javadoc adds that a processor called in one round is called in every later round, including the last, even with no annotations for it, and that javac creates the processor object once per compile, not once per round. That is why `found` carries the commands from round to round.
The Filer Creates Each File Once and Never Replaces a Class That Exists

The first section's processor returns early only when `annotations` is empty, so it writes `CommandIndex` in every call that has `@Command` classes. With `CrudProcessor` in the build, that is rounds 1 and 2:

Note: round 1: roots [Customer, Main, Refund], @Command [Refund], over=false
Note: round 2: roots [CommandIndex, DeleteCustomer], @Command [DeleteCustomer], over=false
error: javax.annotation.processing.FilerException: Attempt to recreate a file for type app.CommandIndex
Note: round 3: roots [], @Command [], over=true
1 error

A file can be created once per compile; the second `createSourceFile` throws. The build broke only because another processor's output carried `@Command`: a project without `@Crud` builds fine with the same processor. Had the second write been skipped instead, the index would have compiled without `delete-customer`.
The fix keeps collecting in every round and writes once, when `processingOver()` is true:

Note: round 3: roots [], @Command [], over=true
warning: File for type 'app.CommandIndex' created in the last round will not be subject to annotation processing.
1 warning
$ java -cp out/app app.Main delete-customer
customer deleted

`CommandIndex` has no annotations, so no processor needs to see it, and javac still compiled it. With `-Werror` the same compile failed on that warning, so a build that sets it must write the file earlier, from a round it can tell is the last to bring `@Command` classes. A generated file whose annotations a processor must see has to be written before the last round.
The same rule protects the user's classes. A processor that creates a source file named `app.Refund`, to replace it with a version that logs, gets:

app/src/app/Refund.java:6: error: javax.annotation.processing.FilerException: Attempt to recreate a file for type app.Refund
public class Refund implements Runnable {
       ^
1 error

The `Filer` javadoc counts the initial inputs as created by a "zeroth round", so they can't be created again. Nor can a processor edit a class in place: `Element` has only getters. (Lombok adds methods to the classes being compiled by working on javac's internal syntax trees, outside this API.) The `Filer` javadoc's alternative is to generate a subclass of the user's class, or a superclass that the user's class names in its own `extends`.

Summary

items: **A processor is code javac runs during the compile.** It reads declarations, not objects, and what it adds are new files that compile with the sources. Name it with `-processor` or a processor path: javac 25 no longer runs one found only on the class path.

**Report errors through the `Messager` with the element.** javac then points at the user's line. Without the element there is no location, and an error in generated code points at a file nobody wrote.
**Processing runs in rounds.** A generated file is processed in the next round, and one processor object sees every round, the last with `processingOver()` true.
**The `Filer` creates each file once and never replaces an input.** An aggregate file written per round fails with `FilerException` once a later round brings more; collect in a field and write once.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The check found a private constructor. List what else `new X()` in generated code needs from `X` (not abstract, not an inner class, type arguments), and which of these a `Messager` check reports more clearly than the compile of the generated file.

Your build compiles only the files that changed. The aggregate index then sees only those files' `@Command` classes. What do the `Filer`'s "originating elements" give an incremental build, and what must still be compiled in full?
Compare a build with `IndexProcessor` to a startup scan with reflection, for a service with 400 commands: measure the compile time added and the startup time saved on your machine.

blocks.text: Design Note: Why a Processor Can Only Add Files

JSR 269 gives a processor a read-only model of the program and a `Filer` that refuses to touch the inputs. The API offers no way to change a class the developer wrote, and generated code sits in files that can be opened, read and diffed.

The cost falls on the design of the user's code: code that wants generated behaviour must call a generated class (`CommandIndex.create`) or extend one. Lombok changes the class itself, which ties it to javac's internals.
